prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In Tunis we try to discuss divorce And dying but give up to lounge With rug merchants under a plum tree. From its corner the lamb’s severed head Watches the flies drink from its eyes And its fat disappear into the fire. The light rinses the edge of your sandal, The two wasps that ornament the blur Of screened window. My grandmother Would have loved a night like this. In the wind chimes I can hear her tea cart With its china rolling through Cook Street’s Stony yard one summer when I was always Thirsty, and she moved like a figure On a clock from my lawn chair to the cart, Or swabbed me with alcohol, or cut My hair with the straight razor. I was a week out of the hospital. Beneath my breasts an incision was crossed With stitches of surgical thread. The scalpel came so close it gave My heart a quick kiss. I nearly died. Years later I can still see the skin Flutter on the inside of my left breast And my heart limps like a great uncle Who, because he was a Jew and lame, Was dragged by cossacks across the steppes. He became a friend asking a favor Of a horse who ran so hard, so perfectly Hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.

In Tunis we attempt to speak of divorce
And of dying, but relent, and lounge instead
With rug merchants beneath a plum tree.
From its corner, the lamb's severed head
Watches the flies drink from its eyes
As its fat dissolves into the fire.
The light bathes the edge of your sandal,
The two wasps that adorn the blur
Of the screened window. My grandmother
Would have cherished a night like this.
In the wind chimes I can hear her tea cart,
Its china rattling across Cook Street's
Stony yard, one summer when I was forever
Thirsty, and she moved like a figure
On a clock from my lawn chair to the cart,
Or swabbed me with alcohol, or trimmed
My hair with the straight razor.
I was a week out of the hospital.
Beneath my breasts an incision was laced
With stitches of surgical thread.
The scalpel came so close it grazed
My heart with a fleeting kiss. I nearly died.
Years later I can still see the skin
Flutter on the inner side of my left breast,
And my heart limps like a great-uncle
Who, because he was a Jew and lame,
Was dragged by cossacks across the steppes.
He became a friend imploring a favor
Of a horse who ran so hard, so perfectly
Hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.

Here's my rewrite:

While staying in Tunis, we attempt to talk about divorce and mortality, but abandon the effort and relax instead beneath a plum tree, keeping company with carpet sellers. Off in one corner, a lamb's cut-off head observes flies sipping from its eyes, while its fat melts away into the flames. Sunlight washes over the border of your sandal, along with the pair of wasps that decorate the haze of the screened window. A night such as this would have delighted my grandmother. Within the chiming of the wind, I catch the sound of her tea cart, its dishes rattling across the rocky courtyard on Cook Street, during a certain summer when thirst never left me, and she traveled—like a clock's mechanical figure—from where I sat in my lawn chair over to the cart, or dabbed me clean with alcohol, or trimmed my hair using the straight razor.

Only seven days earlier I'd left the hospital. Below my breasts, a cut was laced together with surgical stitching. The blade had passed so near that it brushed my heart like a swift kiss. Death had nearly claimed me. Even now, all these years afterward, I can watch the skin quiver along the inner side of my left breast, and my heart moves with a limp—like some great-uncle who, being both Jewish and crippled, was hauled by cossacks over the vast plains. He turned into a companion, requesting a kindness from a horse that galloped with such force, such flawless intensity, that the green grass climbed upward to greet him.
outputs.L3:
**Beneath the Plum Tree**

I sit in Tunis among the rug merchants, cross-legged beneath a plum tree, and for once I have set aside the heavy talk. The weighty conversations—of divorce, of death, of all the ruptures that press against a life—I have abandoned them for a while. Here there is only leisure, the slow unspooling of an afternoon, the merchants laughing among their bright bolts of wool and silk.

Then the wind stirs, and somewhere a set of chimes begins its delicate, aimless music. The sound undoes me. All at once I am no longer here but far away and long ago, a child on Cook Street, convalescing under my grandmother's patient care. I can almost feel the cool sheets, the quiet of the sickroom, the way she moved through those days like a soft and constant light. The chimes have carried her back to me whole.

For I was recovering, then, from something grave. A surgery that ran close—too close—to the heart, the surgeon's blade passing near the very center of me. I bear the incision still, a pale seam across my chest, the mark of how nearly I slipped over the edge. It was a brush with death in the truest sense, that early nearness to my own ending.

And so my heart has been a damaged thing ever since, a wounded and halting muscle. When I think of it, I think of my great uncle—a lame Jewish man from the old country, dragged by cossacks across the endless steppes. His crippled leg, my crippled heart: both broken, both hauled roughly through a world that showed them no mercy.

I imagine his last moments even now. The horse running, running, faster than any body could endure, until at the end the green grass itself seemed to rise up from the earth to meet him—rushing upward as he fell, as if the whole living field had bent to gather him in.
outputs.L4:
The poem opens with the speaker at ease, resting beneath a plum tree in Tunis, the warmth and stillness of the setting inviting a kind of reverie. In this drowsy, sun-soaked moment, the boundaries of the present begin to loosen, and the speaker slips backward into memory. The mind wanders first to a beloved grandmother, a figure whose presence still lingers with tenderness, and then to a more harrowing recollection: a near-fatal surgery. The operation left its mark not only on the body but on the psyche, a scar carved close to the heart—both literally, as a physical trace, and figuratively, as a reminder of how narrowly death was avoided.

From this intimate personal history, the poem widens its scope. The image of the "limping heart"—wounded, laboring, marked by survival—becomes a bridge between the individual and the ancestral. The speaker's damaged heart transforms into the figure of a lame ancestor, a man dragged by cossacks, evoking a legacy of persecution, violence, and endurance that stretches back through generations. Here the personal wound and the collective historical wound merge; the scar near the speaker's heart carries within it the inherited suffering of a family and a people.

Yet the poem does not end in pain or paralysis. Instead, it moves toward release and transcendence. The lame ancestor, the dragged and suffering figure, gives way to an image of a horse running with such force and abandon that "the green grass rose to meet him." This final image is one of liberation—of momentum overtaking injury, of life surging up to embrace the runner even in the midst of hardship. The rising grass suggests both a physical rush of the world coming forward and a kind of spiritual welcome, a reconciliation between the living body and the earth that receives it.

Taken as a whole, the poem weaves together mortality, memory, and family history into a meditation on survival. It acknowledges the fragility of the body and the weight of inherited trauma, yet insists on the possibility of endurance and grace. What begins as quiet rest beneath a plum tree becomes a profound reckoning with the past—and, ultimately, an affirmation that even a limping heart can find its way into motion, carried forward by the momentum of life itself.
outputs.L5:
# Discovering Tunis

Tunis, the vibrant capital of Tunisia, is a city where history and modernity blend seamlessly. Situated along the Mediterranean coast, Tunis welcomes visitors with its rich culture, warm hospitality, and stunning architecture.

## A City of Contrasts

Walking through Tunis, you will find ancient medinas standing proudly alongside modern boulevards. The historic Medina of Tunis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is filled with narrow streets, bustling souks, and beautiful mosques. Here, tradition and daily life come together in a colorful tapestry of sights and sounds.

## Culture and Cuisine

Tunis is a place best explored with an open heart and a curious spirit. The city offers delicious cuisine, combining fresh seafood, aromatic spices, and traditional dishes that reflect its unique heritage. Local markets are brimming with fresh produce, handmade crafts, and friendly vendors eager to share their stories.

## Things to Do

Visitors to Tunis can enjoy many attractions, including:

- **The Bardo Museum**, filled with ancient mosaics and artifacts
- **Sidi Bou Said**, a charming village with blue and white buildings
- **Carthage**, home to remarkable ruins and archaeological wonders

## A Warm Welcome

Whether you come for the history, the food, or simply to relax by the sea, Tunis greets everyone with open arms. It is a destination that stays with you long after you leave, inviting you to return again and again.

Come and experience Tunis—a city full of life, beauty, and endless discovery.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem set in Tunis that begins with a lazy afternoon among rug merchants and drifts into memories of the speaker's grandmother and a childhood surgery near the heart.
counterfactuals.output:
# Threads

In Tunis the afternoon lies down
like a cat in a doorway,
and the rug merchants have stopped
pretending to sell.
They drink mint tea the color of old brass
and let the wool speak for itself—
crimson, indigo, the burnt orange
of a sun too tired to set.

One merchant unrolls a carpet
with a snap of his wrists
and the dust rises like a held breath released,
and I am seven again,
watching my grandmother's hands
shuttle thread through the frame of her loom,
her fingers knotting what the mouth could not.

She had a word for everything
except the things that mattered.
*Habibti,* she'd say, meaning
*sit closer,* meaning
*I have already outlived my own mother,*
meaning *the pattern only makes sense from behind.*

The wool here smells of lanolin and smoke
and I remember the hospital gown,
the paper slippers,
the doctor pointing to the diagram of a chest
and the small blue country of the heart—
*just here,* he said,
*a hair's breadth from where we'll cut.*

I was too young to be afraid,
so my grandmother was afraid for me,
her worry a rug she wove all night
in the waiting room,
each row a prayer she didn't believe would work
but offered anyway.

They opened me
near the place a child keeps its courage
and closed me up again
and left a seam so faint
you'd have to know to look for it.

Now the merchant asks if I am buying.
I run my thumb along a border
where the weaver made a deliberate flaw—
because only God, my grandmother told me,
is permitted to finish anything perfectly.

I think of her hands, long stilled.
I think of my own scar,
that quiet knot
holding the whole design together
from behind,
where no one thinks to look.

I buy nothing.
I carry it all out
into the ordinary light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary lyric poem that moves associatively from a foreign travel scene to a personal medical trauma and finally to an ancestor persecuted for being Jewish.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salt, Anointing**

In Lisbon the tiles are the blue of a held breath,
and the woman selling figs
presses one open with her thumb
so I can see the red seeds constellate
like something spilled and never wiped.
I take it in my mouth. It tastes of iron.

Iron—the word swings me back
to the table where they laid me flat,
the overhead lamp a foreign sun,
and the technician saying *hold very still now*
as the dye went cold-blue through the vein,
mapping me, the body's private tilework
lit from inside, each chamber
a little room I'd never been allowed to enter.
I lay there being read. I lay there
translated into weather, into shadow.
*We found something,* they said,
the way you'd say it of a coin
turned up in a field, or a name
scratched into the underside of a pew.

And the name is what carries me down again,
past the machines, past the figs,
to the town whose spelling changed
each time the border did—
where my great-grandfather kept his ledger
in a language they later made a crime.
They came for him with paper first,
then fire. He wore the yellow the way
the fig wears its bruise: from within,
marked, edible, made to be opened
by another's thumb.

I don't know where they put his body.
I know only that some inheritance
runs cold and blue beneath the skin,
that I am the room they walk through now,
the held breath, the tile,
the still-warm seed
survival scattered
and could not, in the end, wipe clean.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about a heart operation and near-death experience, weaving in vivid sensory images of a lamb's severed head, wasps on a screened window, and a grandmother's tea cart.
counterfactuals.output:
Under the Anesthesia

They wheeled me under, and the world dissolved
to something older than my own two hands—

my grandmother's kitchen, the tea cart's silver wheels
squeaking across linoleum, that gleam
of the pot she never let go cold.
The steam rose like a soul deciding.

Then the lamb's head on the butcher's block,
its eyes gone opal, patient, unafraid,
the severed neck a garden of dark roses.
I was six. I did not look away.
I learned then what the body is:
a room the light gets out of.

On the porch, the wasps against the screen—
that dry electric hum, that wanting in,
their bodies knocking, knocking at the mesh,
the way my heart knocked at its cage of bone
while gloved hands cupped it, held it still,
and stopped it, as you'd stop a clock
to fix the broken hour inside.

I hovered there. The wasps grew loud.
The tea cart rolled its bright wheel toward me.
The lamb regarded me with its blind mercy.
Somewhere a machine sang one long note—

and then the pump, the pull, the tide
returning to the emptied shore.
My chest a struck bell. My grandmother
pouring, always pouring, the amber arc
that would not, would not reach the cup.

I woke. The screen still held its wasps at bay.
The world came back in copper and in ache.
I keep them all now in the same drawer:
the head, the hum, the wheel, the wound—
the proof that I was carried to the door,
and set back down, and told: not yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a meditative, image-rich poem in the style of Jorie Graham or Larry Levis, blending place, memory, illness, and family history into a single unbroken stanza.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inheritance, or the Body as a House Left Open

Consider how the light comes through my grandmother's kitchen even now, years after they sold the house in Ohio, how it falls across a table that no longer exists and finds the flour still suspended in her hands, the way she never stopped moving until the stroke arrived like weather no one forecast, and I am thinking of this while the IV drips its slow arithmetic into my arm, each drop a small erasure, and outside the window a mockingbird performs its borrowed songs, all mimicry, all memory, the way I've become a kind of archive of the dead, carrying my father's cough, my mother's insomnia, the particular blue that darkens under my eyes at dusk the same blue that pooled beneath her eyes when she forgot my name and called me by her sister's, dead since 1962, and isn't the body just this—a rented room where the previous tenants left their furniture, their fingerprints on every surface, the diabetes coiled in the blood like a letter I never asked to receive, and I remember the well behind the farmhouse, how you could drop a stone and count the seconds before the small applause of water, how my grandfather said the water tasted of iron because the earth there kept its wounds close, and now the nurse checks my chart, her pen a tiny oar rowing across the paper, and I want to tell her about the peonies, how they only open when the ants come to loosen them, how nothing arrives into its beauty alone, how even dying we are attended, and the afternoon leans its long shadow through the blinds, striping the sheets like a field newly plowed, and somewhere the flour is still falling, the hands still working the dough into the shape of hunger's answer, and I close my eyes and it is Ohio, it is 1979, it is the smell of yeast and the radio's low murmur, and my grandmother is telling me to wash my hands before I touch anything, as if the body were something that could be kept clean, as if we do not spend our whole lives being slowly claimed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that opens in North Africa discussing divorce and dying, then spirals into recollection and ends with a lame Jewish great-uncle and a running horse meeting green grass.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Desert Keeps**

In Tunisia the heat divides a marriage
the way it splits the clay—no violence,
only the slow unclasping of two hands
that held too long. My mother signs
the papers under an awning in Sfax,
and somewhere in a whitewashed room
a stranger I once called father is dying,
his lungs full of a sea he never crossed.

Divorce and dying: the two verbs
the desert conjugates all afternoon.
I watch the light go amber on the salt flats
and I am suddenly nine again, then six,
then folded back into a photograph
where everyone is laughing and nobody
knows the ending yet. Memory works
like this—a spiral, not a line,
each loop returning smaller, tighter,
until it finds the single seed
around which all the years have coiled.

And there he is. Great-Uncle Mordecai,
who left Odessa with a limp and a prayer book,
one leg shorter, dragging like a comma
that refused to end the sentence of his life.
He kept a horse he was too lame to ride—
a bony thing the color of old bread—
and every spring he'd lead it, both of them
uneven, hobbling, to the one green field
that Poland offered like an apology.

I never saw it. I have only the story,
passed hand to hand until it wore smooth,
but I can watch it now across the salt:
the old man loosens the rope, steps back,
and the horse remembers what a horse is for.
It runs. It runs the way the dying can't,
the way a marriage doesn't, the way memory
runs backward into all that green—
and Mordecai just stands there, laughing,
his bad leg planted in the living grass,
watching something whole and fast and free
arrive at last, and arrive, and arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
